claims.text: The starting material is bulk, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr with inherent chemical disorder.
A sample set contains a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
Explicitly incorporating intrinsic chemical disorder and oxygen-induced defects will produce conductivity predictions closer to experiment than defect-free analytical models.
The proposed predictive approach will explicitly represent point defects and oxygen impurities in calculations of electronic conductivity.
Defect scattering dominates electron transport in HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Over 300–1200 K, phonon scattering combines with defect scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen induces defects and associated local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced defects and lattice distortions increase electron scattering and alter effective carrier mobility relative to a perfect crystal.
Oxygen impurities and other defects introduce resistive contributions absent from defect-free analytical calculations.
Representing defects and lattice distortions allows the model to capture low-temperature defect scattering and high-temperature phonon–defect interactions.
The defect-inclusive model will predict lower conductivity than defect-free analytical models.
The defect-inclusive model will predict a different temperature dependence of conductivity than defect-free analytical models.
The model is expected to reduce prediction error by more than 20% relative to the analytical baseline.
Traditional analytical conductivity models used as the baseline assume perfect, defect-free crystal structures.
The claimed improvement applies to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Comparable improvement may not occur outside the stated oxygen-content and temperature limits.
Model performance may vary with defect distribution and processing history.
Failure to reduce conductivity-prediction error by at least 10% relative to the defect-free baseline across both temperature regimes will falsify the hypothesis.
